Act I · 15 July

The itch.The itch.

A spec with twelve decisions, written the day before. Its plan lasted about a day.

I

I

Act I

The spec was wrong in a day but still did its job.

The spec saidWhat shippedWhen Speech to textwhisper.cpp with CoreMLApple’s SpeechAnalyzerDay one SummariesLlama 3.2 3B via MLXApple’s Foundation ModelsDay one Minimum macOS14, Sonoma26, Apple silicon onlyDay one CalendarNot in version 1An up-next card, auto-recordCycle 14 NetworkOff, permanentlyOn, for model downloads onlyDay four

What survived, untouched

  • Local by construction.
  • Calm, not surveillance.
  • Your notes stay yours.
  • Markdown as the common language.
  • Degrade gracefully.
What I learned

Hold principles tightly and technology loosely. The technology will change first.

Act I · The itch

6

Act I · decided on day one

The best decision was a constraint.

  1. I chose

    macOS 26 and Apple silicon only

  2. So

    macOS brings the speech and language models

  3. So

    Nothing to download when you install

  4. So

    No server to run

  5. So

    No subscription to justify

What it cost

Fewer people can run it. I chose that on day one and wrote it down.

What it bought

A privacy claim you can check, and no monthly fee.

What I learned

Look for a constraint that removes work. Mine removed the server, the downloads and the subscription.

Receipt Decision O2, 15 July

Forty unrelated rows became one series with continuity and cadence. It was the project’s largest design cycle.

Act III · 18 to 23 July

The reckoning.The reckoning.

The best line in the pitch stopped being true, and nobody had noticed.

III

III

Act III

Then I broke my own promise.

decisions.mdD8

No outbound network entitlement. The privacy promise is structurally impossible to break.

No longer true18 July

Optional transcription models had to be downloaded, so the network entitlement went on and the best line in the pitch became false.

Nobody had noticed, and the cheap fix was to soften the wording and move on.

Act III · The reckoning

13

Act III · five days later

So I made it narrower, and harder to break.

Your meeting content never leaves this Mac.

I rewrote every sentence to name its actor (GRØD, macOS or another app) and banned the old sentence by name.

One door

Of 479 source files, one may open the network. A test reads the source and fails the build if a second one tries.

Every square is a file in GRØD’s source.

What I learned

Don’t leave what matters to memory. A page waits to be read. A check in the process finds the next person for you.

Receipt NetworkChokePointTests

Act III · The reckoning

14

Act IV · 25 July

The turn.The turn.

Ten days in, I had a beautiful app that only worked on one machine, so I stopped adding things.

IV

IV

The 1.0 bar, written 25 July and unchanged since.

Never loses a meeting, and a stranger can install it.Never loses a meeting, and a stranger can install it.

Both clauses can be tested in the field, and neither can be gamed. It stopped the delight work and put everything into hardening.

What I learned

“95% capture success” starts a negotiation. A sentence tells you what to do on a Tuesday.

Receipt It is why onboarding blocks the release.

Act IV · The turn

16

Act IV · how the work ran

Five lanes, one gate. The gate was me.

What I learned

Once building got cheap, my job became deciding what has to happen first and where the boundaries sit.

Receipt The lane landing entries, decisions.md

Each lane ran on its own to merge-ready. Plausible work can merge cleanly and still be wrong in combination, and that is what the gate caught.

Act IV · The turn

17

Act IV · the division that settled

Who owned what.

MeThe agents What the product isWhat the code is Whether a decision is rightWhether it is consistent Every mergeEvery branch, up to merge-ready Taste, and when something is shoutingCoverage, and the long tail Knowing when to stopNot knowing when to stop

What the agents got wrong, in their own words

  • Read a tool that reported nothing as proof that nothing happened.
  • Fixed the same race four times before looking for the family.
  • Called work verified when a command had only exited zero.
What I learned

I couldn’t review 106,000 lines of Swift. I could review what 153,000 lines of tests promised.

Receipt The agent’s own write-up, 08-how-we-worked.md

Act V · 5 to 13 August

The subtraction.The subtraction.

I deleted one feature on purpose and kept putting off one piece of work.

V

V

Act V · deleted 5 August

Quick Peek

It was named in the spec, shipped in cycle five and liked. Then opening a meeting became free, and the preview saved one gesture while showing less.

“A regression nobody notices is a feature nobody uses.”

What I learned

Before you can delete a feature, you need a record of why it exists and some sign that it’s dead.

Receipt decisions.md, 5 August

Act V · The subtraction

21

Act V

What I’d do differently.

Onboarding lost every prioritisation contest for weeks, because I’d been a user for months and the stranger never had.

So it went first and blocked the release. Now the first run asks you to say something, and shows you.

What I learned

The first five minutes lose every contest they enter, so schedule them first or let them block the release.

Receipt Lesson 10, in my own write-up

Epilogue · Breakfast

25

Generosity

What I’m bringing back to the practice.

  • The cycle

    Brainstorm, spec, plan, build, then write down why. A way to run agent-built work that someone else can audit.

  • Lanes and a gate

    Agents in parallel without the mess: each lane stops at merge-ready, and a person merges.

  • Checks, not pages

    Building what a client must never lose into how the team works, so nobody has to remember it.

  • Lessons with receipts

    Ten of mine, and the agents’ own account of what went wrong.

Ask me for any of them.
